abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. Besides ruling out the existence of sluggish diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt nanoalloys and lowering their temperature range of application, the study allows distinguishing kinetic and thermodynamic effects on their structural properties, which is an essential prerequisite to better control the synthesis of complex nanomaterials.

In situ transmission electron microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate the thermal behavior of FCC AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles from 298 to 973 K. The formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of nanostructures are revealed at high temperatures, shedding new light on the structural properties and thermal stability of high‐entropy nanoalloys.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In this context, studying the thermal behavior of HENA is a necessary first step to evaluate their structural stability with the view to better target their potential high‐temperature applications. Moreover, our current state of knowledge on atomic diffusion in HENA is still far from complete, and experimental evidence of the existence of sluggish diffusion in HENA is lacking. In the present work, we used in situ scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), corroborated with atomistic simulations, to study in real‐time and at the atomic scale the structural and compositional evolution of AuCoCuNiPt NPs from 298 to 973 K. These in situ insights into the thermodynamic properties of AuCoCuNiPt HENA reveal their poor structural stability at high temperature due to atomic diffusion that cannot be considered as sluggish.

sec.title: In Situ Heating STEM Investigations
sec.p:
AuCoCuNiPt NPs were fabricated by Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) directly on the amorphous 50 nm thick SiN film of a heating TEM microchip (Figure
1a, see Experimental Section).[
2a
] Particle diameter in the as‐prepared sample ranges from 3–6.5 nm with a mean diameter of 4.5 nm (Figure 1b). Prior to heating, the composition of individual NPs was measured by energy dispersive X‐ray spectroscopy (EDS) in STEM mode (Figure S1, Supporting Information). The spider plot in Figure 1c shows that particle composition is uniform and ≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21 with a dispersion below 5%. EDS chemical maps revealed the homogenous distribution of the five metals in the NPs (Figure S2a, Supporting Information), and the Face Centered Cubic (FCC) structure of NPs assembly was confirmed by electron diffraction (Figure S2b, Supporting Information). High‐resolution imaging was exploited to identify the various shapes of as‐grown NPs. To improve data quality, NPs fabricated on 5 nm‐thick carbon film were also analyzed but the shape and structure of HENA are similar on both substrates (Figure S2, Supporting Information). Small monocrystalline FCC NPs with a Wulff shape can be found but most HENA present a multi‐twinned structure, including some decahedra and many icosahedra that are clearly identified when they are observed along their two‐, three‐ or five‐fold axes. (Figure 1d–e; Figure S2c–j, Supporting Information).

We then combined the high spatial resolution of aberration‐corrected STEM and large solid‐angle energy dispersive X‐ray spectroscopy to follow the size, shape, atomic structure, and composition of these HENA from 298 to 973 K. In Figure
2a, a temperature‐series of STEM HAADF images shows the growth and reshaping behavior of an assembly of NP after 15 min at 473, 67, 773, and 973 K. Particle size distribution remains unchanged at 473 K but it is impacted when the temperature reaches 673 K (Figure 2b). Thermo‐activated growth mechanisms lead to the progressive loss of the smallest NPs (between 2 and 4 nm) and a widening of the size distribution up to 13 nm, at 973 K. It is also notable that the NP density decreases sharply with increasing temperature. Aside from their growth, NPs also reshape upon annealing. Indeed, the in‐plane shape ratio of NPs (i.e., the ratio between the minimum and maximum radii of NPs) increases with temperature, indicating that NPs are evolving from elliptical shapes to spherical ones (Figure 2c).

caption.p: Size and shape evolution during thermal annealing. a) STEM HAADF images showing the evolution of NPs over time at different temperatures, given in the top right corner of each image. All the pictures show the same area 15 min after reaching the temperature step. Evolution of b) the size distribution and c) the shape ratio (i.e., ratio between the in‐plane min and max radii) of NPs over temperature.

sec.p:
The growth mechanisms of HENA are here mainly driven by coalescence phenomena that activate when the temperature is above 673 K. The size of NPs may also be slightly affected by Ostwald ripening, but as the dissolution of small nanoparticles was never observed during the in situ heating experiments, we assume that the effect of these coarsening mechanisms is negligible. Evidently, coalescence phenomena speed up as the temperature rises. At 773 and 873 K coalescence and reshaping occur in several minutes (Figure
3a,b) while at 973 K it lasts only a few seconds (Figure 3c). Interestingly, phase separation is frequently observed during the coalescence of two sup‐5 nm NPs at 773 and 873 K. As illustrated in the STEM HAADF images in Figure 3a,b, high‐contrast areas appear at the surface of just merged NPs. These heterogenous contrasts evidence the segregation of metals with different atomic numbers during coalescence events and they are still observed after the subsequent reshaping of the coalesced nanostructures (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Moreover, STEM‐EDS mapping performed at the single NP scale revealed that 5 nm NPs that did not coalesce maintained a well‐homogenous distribution of all metals (Figure 4a), but the high‐contrast areas observed in larger coalesced NPs are exclusively made of Au‐Cu (Figure 4b). These results suggest that atomic diffusion within the nanostructures at 773 and 873 K tends to segregate Au and Cu at the surface but the resulting Janus configuration can be only observed in coalesced nanostructures in which atom mobility is more important. At 973 K, atomic diffusion is active enough to drive a phase separation in all nanostructures. Indeed, just after raising the temperature from 873 to 973 K, all the NPs reduce in size. As this phenomenon overlaps with the coalescence that is very active at 973 K, this size decrease is not captured in the size distribution measured after 15 min at 973 K (Figure 2b). However as shown in Figure 3d,e, we measure a size reduction of 22% of all the observed NPs within the first minutes at 973 K. Accordingly, a complete loss of gold and copper is evidenced by STEM‐EDS, while at lower temperatures the composition of NPs was quite stable (Figure 3f and Figure S4, Supporting Information). The loss of Au and Cu from the NPs at 973 K is most likely due to the segregation of these two metals at the NP surface followed by the melting and evaporation of the Au‐Cu shell. It is worth noting that Au and Cu have the lowest melting temperature of the five metals (Table S1, Supporting Information) and the melting of Au, Cu, and AuCu NPs was also observed by TEM at 973 K in previous reports.[
9
]

caption.p: Structural and compositional dynamics of HENA under annealing. Coalescence events of NPs recorded in real‐time by STEM HAADF at a) 773 K, b) 873 K, c) 973 K. The acquisition time is indicated in the top left corner of each image. The high Z‐contrast areas suggesting the phase separation of metals are indicated by white arrows. STEM HAADF images of the same area recorded d) right after reaching 973 K and e) 3 min later, showing the size decrease of NPs due to the evaporation of gold and cooper. The size of some NPs in nm is indicated in both images. f) Evolution of the mean composition of individual NPs measured by STEM‐EDX nano‐analysis.

Chemical mapping of HENA at different temperatures. (left to right) STEM HAADF image and EDS elemental maps of the NP framed in white on the STEM HAADF image. EDS elemental maps showing the spatial distribution of CoPtNi and AuCu alloys in the NP and EDS intensity profiles measured along the arrow seen on STEM HAADF images. a) CoNiCuPtAu NP with homogeneous contrast that has not undergone coalescence at 773K. b) CoNiCuPtAu NP with inhomogeneous contrast that has undergone coalescence at 773K and c) NP with homogenous contrast at 973 K in which only Co, Ni, Pt are detected.

sec.p: The resulting distribution of Co, Ni, and Pt within the NPs at 973K is still homogeneous (Figure 4c) and these ternary nanoalloys remain crystalline. Indeed, high‐resolution imaging shows that NPs keep their FCC structure from room temperature to 973 K (Figures S5–S7, Supporting Information). Crystal‐defect density increases with temperature since the proportion of monocrystalline NPs decreases from 30% at 473 K to 20% at 773 K (Figure S8, Supporting Information). This is likely due to the coalescence phenomena that can lead to the formation of twinned nanocrystals when two NPs in different orientation merge together.

sec.title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations

caption.p: MD simulations investigating the thermal behavior of a 4 nm CoNiCuPtAu NP containing 2057 atoms in an icosahedral structure. a) Equilibrium configurations at different temperatures. The left column presents the shell views and the right one the cross‐section views perpendicular to the five‐fold axis of the icosahedra. b) Evolution of the surface concentration as a function of the temperature. The dotted line represents the equiatomic concentration. c) Local energies of each metal atoms in histogram forms at 800 and 1100K.

MD simulations investigating the effects of coalescence on the thermal behavior of CoNiCuPtAu NPs. a–f) Snapshots of the atomic configurations during the coalescence of two NPs containing 2057 atoms at 1200 K. g) Comparison of the Au concentration on the surface of a single and a double (i.e coalesced) icosahedral NP. h) Self‐diffusivity of Au atoms as a function of the temperature measured in the whole coalesced NP (global) and in the neck area around the interface between the two coalesced icosahedra as shown in blue in the scheme.
